ml.title: Machine learning foundations
ml.lede: The theory that every AI-engineer loop still tests, whatever the job title says. Each topic is written as an answer you could give out loud, with the figure you would draw on the whiteboard.

dl.title: Deep learning mechanics
dl.lede: How networks actually train, fail, and scale. Enough depth to debug a run out loud rather than recite a definition.

llm.title: LLMs and generative AI
llm.lede: Tokenisation through serving — the section that decides an AI-engineer offer. Every topic carries the written explanation, an interactive figure where one helps, a numeric exercise to work before you read the answer, and a short reading list of checked sources.

aieng.title: AI engineering in production
aieng.lede: Architecture, cost, monitoring and governance. The senior signal is not knowing what a transformer is — it is knowing what breaks at 3am and what it costs.

ts.title: Time series & AI
ts.lede: From the basics to foundation models, in the order you would learn them: what makes temporal data different, decomposition and stationarity, the classical baselines, honest backtesting, feature-based and deep models, uncertainty, zero-shot foundation models, anomaly detection, hierarchies and causal questions — and how a forecasting system runs in production. Each topic has a worked exercise, quick checks and checked sources; the figures in topics 3 and 5 are interactive.

classic.title: Classic system design
classic.lede: The eighteen “design X” cases every loop still asks. Each one is written as a walkthrough you can actually deliver in sixty minutes — a beginner’s primer on the domain, a timed structure from scoping to close, the deep dive the interviewer will pick, the senior layer above it, and a sizing exercise to work before you read the answer.
classic.note: Follow the clock strip at the top of each case. Scope and agree the requirements (5 min) → do the arithmetic out loud (7) → API and data model (8) → draw the architecture (10) → the one deep dive that decides the round (16) → scale, failure and trade-offs (10) → close with the sentence you want them to remember (4). Drive it yourself; silence is the failure mode.

infra.title: Infrastructure building blocks
infra.lede: The primitives every other design assumes exists. A queue, a key-value store, a cache, a scheduler, a metrics pipeline, object storage, a coordination service — plus the stream-counting, experimentation and prefix-search systems that sit on top. Each one is a sixty-minute walkthrough with the same clock, and together they are the vocabulary the product designs are written in.
infra.note: These reward precision over breadth. Get the arithmetic right, name the guarantee you are providing (and the one you are not), and be explicit about the consistency trade-off — in this family of questions, “what happens during a network partition?” is always the follow-up.

hld.title: AI system design
hld.lede: Twenty-seven designs an AI-engineer loop actually asks for. Each one carries requirements, a back-of-envelope estimate, an architecture, the two or three deep dives that decide the round, and the trade-offs to volunteer before you are asked.
hld.note: Six steps, roughly 60 minutes: clarify requirements and scope (5) → estimate scale (5) → high-level architecture (10) → deep dive on the two hardest components (20) → failure modes and operations (10) → trade-offs and what you would do differently (10). Drive it yourself; silence is the failure mode.

lld.title: Machine coding
lld.lede: Small systems, written properly. Interfaces before implementation, the happy path first, then concurrency and failure — and say the trade-off out loud as you make it.
lld.note: Clarify the requirements and write them down (5 min) → sketch the public interface (5) → implement the core (25) → handle concurrency, errors and edge cases (15) → tests and extensions (10). Working and clear beats clever and half-finished.

mlc.title: ML coding
mlc.lede: The round where you implement an ML algorithm from scratch — usually in NumPy, sometimes in plain Python — in 45 minutes, talking through the maths and the shapes as you go. Thirty-two problems, from linear regression and LoRA to CLIP’s contrastive loss, a tiny ViT and an LSTM with hand-written backprop. Each has a beginner primer on the maths, a reference solution with the tests you would write in the room, the senior follow-ups, and an extension exercise with its own tested answer. Every code block on this page is executed by scripts/check_mlc.py, so the solutions are known to run.
mlc.note: Restate the inputs, outputs and shapes, and ask about edge cases (3 min) → write the maths you are implementing as one or two lines (4) → code the straightforward version first, saying each shape aloud (15) → test on an input you can check by hand, or against a brute-force version (8) → vectorise and fix numerical stability (10) → state the complexity and the follow-up you would expect next (5). A correct loop you have tested beats a clever one-liner you have not.

swe.title: Software engineering
swe.lede: The craft a senior engineer is judged on beyond algorithms: design principles and patterns, clean code and error handling, testing strategy, code review, API design, Git and delivery, architecture, refactoring legacy code, concurrency, security, production debugging and technical leadership. Each topic is written at the depth a 4–5-year interview expects, with a review-style exercise, quick checks and checked sources.

py.title: Python for senior engineers
py.lede: The Python an interviewer expects a senior engineer to know cold: the object model and mutability, data-structure costs, scoping and closures, decorators, generators, OOP and the MRO, exceptions and context managers, memory and the GIL, concurrency with threads, processes and asyncio, typing, performance, pytest, packaging, production web services, and the gotchas behind the trick questions. Every predict-the-output exercise was run on CPython 3.12.

scale.title: Engineering at scale
scale.lede: Distributed systems as senior interviews test them: estimation, load balancing, caching, database internals, replication, sharding, consistency, messaging, sagas, resilience, SRE, microservices, Kubernetes, performance, multi-region and data pipelines.

net.title: Networking for senior engineers
net.lede: From the layer model to production debugging: IP and subnets, TCP and QUIC, DNS, HTTP semantics and versions, TLS, proxies and load balancers, real-time protocols, CDNs, sockets, network security and performance.

mm.title: Multimodal AI
mm.lede: Vision, audio and video for AI engineers — Vision Transformers and CLIP, how vision-language models are built and trained, image and video generation, speech recognition and real-time voice agents, document AI, grounding, and how to evaluate and serve multimodal systems. Every topic starts with a beginner primer and ends with the senior layer, a worked exercise, quick checks and checked sources; topic 3 has an interactive image-token calculator.

rs.title: Reasoning models
rs.lede: How models learned to think before answering: chain of thought and test-time compute, sampling, voting and verifiers, reinforcement learning from policy gradients to PPO and GRPO with verifiable rewards, reward models and reward hacking, distilling reasoning into small models, using reasoning models in products, evaluating them without fooling yourself, training long chain-of-thought models end to end from the R1 recipe to small-team plans, their failure modes from overthinking to unfaithful reasoning and reward hacking, and the RL environments and verifiers they are trained against. Every topic has a beginner primer, a senior layer, a worked exercise, quick checks and checked sources; topic 2 has an interactive test-time-compute simulator.

gpu.title: GPU performance for ML engineers
gpu.lede: What actually makes models fast or slow: GPU architecture, the roofline model and arithmetic intensity, FLOPs and memory arithmetic for transformers, number formats from FP32 to FP4, CUDA and tiled kernels, fusion with Triton and torch.compile, FlashAttention, multi-GPU collectives, ZeRO and FSDP, inference latency and throughput modelling, profiling, and choosing hardware by cost per token. Each topic has a beginner primer, a senior layer, a worked calculation, quick checks and checked sources; topic 2 has an interactive roofline.

os.title: Operating systems for engineers
os.lede: From the kernel boundary to production debugging: system calls and context switches, processes and threads, CPU scheduling from FCFS to EEVDF, synchronization and the classic problems, deadlocks and the Banker's algorithm, paging, the TLB and virtual memory, allocation and the OOM killer, file systems and fsync, I/O with epoll and io_uring, IPC and signals, the namespaces and cgroups that make containers, and Linux performance tools from vmstat to eBPF. Classic OS theory for SDE loops, explained through the Linux you run in production.

db.title: Database management systems
db.lede: The theory and internals underneath every data-heavy system: the relational model, keys and ER modelling, normalization from 1NF to BCNF, SQL from joins and NULL semantics to window functions and recursive CTEs, pages, B+ trees and LSM trees, indexing in depth, query planning and EXPLAIN, WAL and ARIES recovery, serializability, MVCC and locking, PostgreSQL versus InnoDB internals, NoSQL data models, columnar warehouses and star schemas, connection pools, N+1 and pagination, zero-downtime migrations, and vector search with pgvector. Goes deeper than the system-design view in Engineering at scale, with SQL you can write live in an interview.

math.title: Math for machine learning
math.lede: The mathematics underneath every other track, taught from school algebra up: probability and Bayes' theorem, distributions, expectation and variance, the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem, estimation by MLE and MAP, hypothesis tests and A/B-testing statistics, vectors, matrices, eigenvalues and the SVD, derivatives, gradients and the chain rule, convexity and Lagrange multipliers, and entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence. Every idea is worked by hand with real numbers, run in NumPy, and pointed forward to where ML uses it.

k8s.title: Docker and Kubernetes
k8s.lede: From a process with namespaces and cgroups to a GPU platform: what docker run really does, image layers and the build cache, small non-root reproducible images, container networking and volumes, registries, digests, signing and SBOMs, the Kubernetes control plane from kubectl apply to a running container, workloads and rolling updates, Services, DNS and the Gateway API, config and persistent storage, requests, limits, QoS and CPU throttling, the autoscalers, Helm, Kustomize and GitOps, systematic debugging, and GPUs, KServe and Ray for ML. The Docker and Kubernetes questions SDE and platform interviews ask, plus the AI-engineer angles.

beh.title: Behavioural interviews for AI engineers
beh.lede: How behavioural rounds are actually scored — signals, rubrics, levelling and the bar raiser — and how to prepare for them: STAR and a story bank, your intro, conflict, failure and feedback, ownership and ambiguity, influence without authority, why this company and the questions to ask, company frameworks from Amazon's Leadership Principles to Netflix's culture memo, and offers and negotiation. Every topic answers one question twice, weak and strong, with what the interviewer writes down after each sentence.

evals.title: AI evaluation and data
evals.lede: How do you know your LLM feature works, and how do you know it still works next week? Eval-driven development and the eval pyramid, building golden sets sized from confidence intervals, metrics for generative output and why BLEU and ROUGE fail, LLM-as-judge and its biases measured against humans, human labelling and inter-annotator agreement, RAG retrieval and groundedness metrics, the statistics of evals (bootstrap, paired tests, power), online A/B tests and implicit feedback, red-teaming and safety evals, synthetic data and model collapse, curating fine-tuning data with MinHash dedup and decontamination, and running all of it in CI and production with gates, tracing, sampling and drift alerts. Every method worked by hand with real numbers.

agent.title: Agentic systems
agent.lede: Design, build, evaluate and run an agent that does real work without burning money or doing damage. When an agent beats a workflow and the 0.95^n maths of multi-step loops, the agent loop on the wire with ReAct, plan-and-execute and reflection, tool design, the Model Context Protocol in its stateless 2026-07-28 revision, context engineering and prompt caching for long runs, memory and memory poisoning, graphs, routers, parallel calls and human checkpoints, multi-agent systems and when they pay, sandboxes for code and computer use, prompt injection and the lethal trifecta, durable execution with retries, journals and idempotent side effects, agent evals with trajectories, simulated users and pass^k, a cost model at 100,000 tasks a day, tracing, failure modes and incident review in production, then interoperability with MCP and A2A 1.0, the agent frameworks compared with the same agent built two ways, and browser and computer-use agents from perception and grounding to OSWorld 2.0. Every design worked with real numbers and current prices.

recsys.title: Search, ranking & recommender systems
recsys.lede: The ML system design round at Meta, Google, Amazon, Netflix and Spotify: design the feed, the search or the recommendations, and improve them. The multi-stage funnel and its latency budget, BM25 and inverted indexes, collaborative filtering with ALS, two-tower retrieval with in-batch negatives and the logQ correction, hybrid search and rank fusion, ranking models from logistic regression to DCN and multi-task heads, learning to rank and cross-encoders, ranking metrics and why offline gains vanish, features and log-and-wait, position bias and counterfactual evaluation, cold start and bandits, re-ranking for diversity, freshness and fairness, interleaving and long-term holdouts, and where LLMs fit at 10,000 queries per second.

auth.title: Authentication, authorisation & identity
auth.lede: The answer to every system design follow-up that starts "and how do users, services and tenants authenticate and get authorised?". Authentication, authorisation and accounting and where each check lives; passwords stored with Argon2id, scrypt and bcrypt costed in guesses per second; sessions, cookies, CSRF and revocation, with this app's own Flask cookie decoded; JWTs with an HS256 signature recomputed by hand and the classic validation bugs; OAuth 2.0 with PKCE as real HTTP requests and what OAuth 2.1 changes; OpenID Connect, SAML and the account-linking pitfalls behind nOAuth; TOTP computed from a secret and timestamp, passkeys and phishing resistance; ACLs, RBAC, ABAC and Zanzibar-style ReBAC with OPA and Cedar; tenant isolation, row-level security and IDOR; SPIFFE, mTLS and workload identity federation; secrets, KMS and envelope encryption; and permission-aware RAG, delegated agent tokens and MCP authorisation — each with a real incident.

cloud.title: Cloud fundamentals
cloud.lede: The answer to "which cloud building blocks would you use, how are they wired and secured, what does it cost, and what happens when a zone or region fails?". Regions, zones and the shared-responsibility model; IAM policy evaluation worked by hand; a three-zone VPC CIDR plan with every traffic path priced; compute choices from VMs to spot to functions, and Lambda against a container at 1 million and 100 million requests; S3 classes, EBS and EFS for datasets, checkpoints and weights; RDS, Aurora and DynamoDB capacity worked for a real read/write rate; queues, topics, buses, streams and Step Functions with their delivery semantics; Terraform state, locking and promotion; RTO and RPO for three DR strategies; CloudWatch, CloudTrail and on-call; a line-by-line bill for a small web app and commitment break-evens; landing zones, guardrails and breach patterns; and GPU capacity, managed ML and LLM APIs with a fine-tuning run costed on-demand versus spot. AWS is the worked example, with GCP and Azure equivalents, every price dated 7 October 2026 from AWS's price files, and a real incident or engineering write-up in every topic.

torch.title: PyTorch in practice
torch.lede: Can you write, debug and speed up real PyTorch training and inference code under interview pressure? Tensors as views over storage, shapes and broadcasting traps, autograd and nn.Module internals, data loading, a correct training loop, mixed precision and memory, exact checkpoints, an 80-line buggy script taken apart for the ML-debugging round, a GPT with a KV cache, DDP and FSDP2 on the wire, the profiler and torch.compile, export and quantisation, and JAX through PyTorch eyes.

dataeng.title: Data engineering for ML
dataeng.lede: How data gets from production systems into correct, reproducible training sets and feature tables — and what breaks at scale: the lake, warehouse and lakehouse, CDC from the write-ahead log, Parquet row groups and encodings measured byte by byte, partitioning, Z-order and compaction, Iceberg and Delta commits and time travel, Spark stages, shuffles, joins and skew, idempotent Airflow pipelines and backfills, watermarks and exactly-once streaming, SCD2 and point-in-time joins, data contracts and lineage, sharded LLM training data, and a worked monthly bill on three engines.

safety.title: AI safety & alignment
safety.lede: Can you reason clearly and honestly about how AI systems fail, how we test for it, and what a responsible launch looks like? Misuse, misalignment, mistakes and structural risk; RLHF, Constitutional AI, model specs and constitutions; specification gaming and sycophancy measured; what the sleeper-agent, alignment-faking and scheming experiments did and did not show; probes, superposition, sparse autoencoders, circuits and steering; dangerous-capability evaluations and uplift trials; the RSP, Preparedness Framework and Frontier Safety Framework compared with versions and dates; classifiers and over-refusal; debate, weak-to-strong and AI control; the EU AI Act, SB 53 and incident reporting; and how to answer safety questions in interviews. Every claim is sourced to the paper or policy text, with demonstrated results kept apart from hypotheses.

product.title: Product & metrics sense
product.lede: What should we build, how do we know it worked, and what do we do when the number moves? The judgement senior ML and AI loops test in every design round: a reusable answer structure, north-star, driver and guardrail metrics and the ratio traps, turning a product goal into a model objective, diagnosing a metric drop with mix shift and Simpson's paradox, funnels, cohorts, retention and LTV, experiment design for networks and marketplaces, making the launch call with intervals and margins, deciding whether a feature should use ML or an LLM at all, designing and measuring AI features, sizing and prioritising, and five full cases timed like a round. Every company in the cases is hypothetical; every real number is sourced.

algo.title: DSA patterns, taught properly
algo.lede: How to recognise which pattern a problem wants and how to build the solution step by step. Each lesson starts from the brute force, explains why the pattern works, traces it by hand, and ends with the templates, traps and interview questions. Read the lesson, then drill its problems in the DSA list.
